verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Paul the apostle, writing with the assistance of Tertius, who served as the letter's scribe.

**Original Audience:** Believers in Rome from both Jewish and Gentile backgrounds who needed unity in the gospel and practical instruction for life together.

**Purpose of the Book:** To explain the gospel of God's righteousness in Christ, unite Jewish and Gentile believers, and show how God's mercy creates a transformed people.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Romans 9–11 considers Israel's place in God's saving purpose and the tragedy of pursuing righteousness through law-keeping rather than receiving God's righteousness in Christ. Paul explains that the saving message is not impossibly distant. It has been brought near through the proclaimed gospel and calls for a response of faith.

In the Roman world, “lord” could describe masters, rulers, and even the emperor. Publicly identifying Jesus as Lord was therefore more than repeating a religious title. It declared ultimate allegiance to the crucified and risen Jesus. Early believers could face social and political pressure for a confession that placed Christ above every earthly authority.

## Study Note

To “confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus” means openly acknowledge that Jesus is Lord. A confession is not a magical formula whose sounds automatically save. It expresses a real transfer of allegiance: Jesus, not self, sin, public opinion, or political power, has the rightful authority over one's life. Genuine confession is public because faith in Christ cannot remain permanently separated from loyalty and identity.

Believing “in thine heart” is also more than accepting a fact intellectually. In biblical language, the heart is the center of thought, trust, desire, and decision. The content of faith is specific: God raised Jesus from the dead. The resurrection confirms that Jesus truly is Lord, that His sacrificial death was victorious, and that God's new creation has begun. Christian faith therefore rests on God's action in history, not on vague optimism.

“Thou shalt be saved” promises rescue to everyone who relies on the risen Lord. The following verses join heart-belief and confession as two aspects of one genuine response; they are not competing steps or a mechanical checklist. Salvation is God's gracious work received through faith. This verse should produce assurance in Christ rather than confidence in the strength of one's emotions or the perfection of one's religious performance.

## Key Lesson

**Saving faith trusts the risen Jesus and openly acknowledges Him as Lord. Salvation rests in God's gracious action through Christ, not in human achievement or empty words.**

## Application

- Is my confession that Jesus is Lord visible in the decisions, loyalties, and priorities of my daily life?

- When assurance feels weak, focus on the risen Christ and God's promise rather than measuring the intensity of my emotions.

- Ask God for a natural opportunity to speak truthfully and humbly about my faith in Jesus.

## Cross References

- Matthew 10:32–33

- Acts 2:32–36

- Romans 4:24–25

- Romans 10:10–13

- 1 Corinthians 15:1–4

## Word Study

- **Confess (Greek: homologeō) —** To agree, acknowledge openly, or declare the same truth; here, to identify Jesus publicly as Lord.

- **Lord (Greek: kyrios) —** Master, ruler, or sovereign. Applied to Jesus, it expresses His divine authority and rightful claim over life.

- **Heart (Greek: kardia) —** The inner center of thought, trust, desire, and decision, not merely emotion.

- **Saved (Greek: sōzō) —** To rescue or deliver, including God's deliverance from sin, judgment, and death through Christ.

## Reflection

The gospel calls for more than admiration of Jesus. I am invited to trust the One God raised from the dead and to live under His authority. My assurance is anchored in what God has done through Christ, while my confession becomes visible in faithful allegiance.

## Prayer

God of salvation, I believe that You raised Jesus from the dead, and I confess Him as Lord. Deepen my trust, expose rival loyalties, and make my life agree with my words. Give me humble courage to identify with Christ and rest my assurance in Your gracious promise. Amen.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Paul the apostle, with Timothy named alongside him in the letter's opening.

**Original Audience:** The church in Corinth and believers throughout Achaia, including people navigating conflict, repentance, suffering, and questions about Paul's ministry.

**Purpose of the Book:** To defend the integrity of Paul's ministry, repair his relationship with the Corinthians, encourage generous faithfulness, and explain how God's power is displayed through weakness and reconciliation.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Corinth was a prosperous, diverse Roman city marked by commerce, status competition, religious pluralism, and moral pressure. Paul's relationship with the church had become painful because some questioned his authority and judged ministry by outward impressiveness. In chapter 5, he explains that Christ's love controls believers and changes how they evaluate both Christ and other people.

Verse 17 follows the declaration that Christ died for all so that those who live should no longer live for themselves. It also leads into the ministry of reconciliation: God was reconciling the world to Himself through Christ and entrusting that message to His people. New creation is therefore both a new identity and a new direction of life.

## Study Note

To be “in Christ” means to be united with Jesus by faith and included in what His death and resurrection accomplish. Christianity is not merely adding better habits to an unchanged identity. The believer now belongs to Christ, receives His righteousness, shares His life, and becomes part of His people. This relationship is the source of transformation.

“A new creature” can also be translated “new creation.” Paul uses language large enough to point beyond private improvement to God's promised renewal of all things. The resurrection of Jesus has begun the new creation, and those united to Him already participate in it. They remain physically within the old world, but its sin, condemnation, and self-centered values no longer possess the final claim over them.

“Old things are passed away” does not mean every bad habit, painful memory, consequence, or struggle disappears immediately. It means the former order no longer defines the believer's standing or destination. “All things are become new” begins a lifelong renewal expressed through repentance, changed relationships, holy desires, and reconciliation. Believers grow by living from the identity God has already given, not by pretending that the work is complete.

## Key Lesson

**Union with Christ gives believers a genuinely new identity and begins God's transforming work in them. The old life no longer has the final word, even though growth continues over time.**

## Application

- Which past label or failure am I allowing to speak more loudly than my identity in Christ?

- Identify one old pattern that contradicts the new life and replace it with a specific act of obedience.

- Take a practical step toward reconciliation where Christ's renewing work should reshape a damaged relationship.

## Cross References

- Isaiah 43:18–19

- Romans 6:4–6

- Galatians 2:20

- Ephesians 4:22–24

- Revelation 21:5

## Word Study

- **In Christ (Greek: en Christō) —** A phrase describing union with Christ, belonging to Him, and sharing in the benefits of His saving work.

- **New (Greek: kainos) —** New in quality or kind, not merely recent in time.

- **Creature / creation (Greek: ktisis) —** Something created; the phrase points to God's act of making life new and beginning His wider renewal.

- **Passed away (Greek: parerchomai) —** To go by, depart, or lose the former controlling place.

## Reflection

My past may explain parts of my story, but it does not own my identity or determine my future. In Christ, God has begun something genuinely new. I can face remaining struggles honestly while choosing habits, relationships, and loyalties that agree with the new creation.

## Prayer

God of new creation, thank You that my identity is now found in Christ. Break the power of old patterns and false labels, renew my desires, and make the change You have begun increasingly visible. Use my life to carry Your reconciliation and hope to others. Amen.

**KJV Study Guide**

*“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Matthew, one of Jesus' twelve apostles and formerly a tax collector, according to the Gospel's traditional attribution.

**Original Audience:** Early Christian readers learning to understand Jesus as Messiah and carry His teaching to all nations.

**Purpose of the Book:** To present Jesus as the promised Messiah and King and commission His followers to make obedient disciples among all peoples.

## Historical & Cultural Context

These are among Jesus' final words in Matthew's Gospel. After His resurrection, the eleven disciples met Him on a mountain in Galilee. Some worshipped while others still wrestled with doubt. Jesus first declared that all authority in heaven and earth belonged to Him; the mission rests on His kingship, not the disciples' confidence or ability.

The command widens the mission to “all nations.” In the first-century world, this required crossing ethnic, linguistic, geographic, and religious boundaries. The disciples were not sent to spread their own culture but to bring people under the teaching and lordship of Jesus.

## Study Note

The central command is to make disciples of all nations. A disciple does more than agree with information or attend a meeting: a disciple learns from Jesus, trusts Him, adopts His way of life, and helps others do the same. Going is part of the mission, whether across the street or across cultures, because discipleship cannot remain turned inward.

Baptism publicly identifies a person with the triune God—Father, Son, and Holy Ghost—and with Jesus' community. It marks a new allegiance and life. The singular “name” joined with Father, Son, and Spirit places all three within the one divine identity proclaimed by the church. Baptism is a sign of God's saving claim and the believer's belonging, not an empty ceremony.

Teaching disciples “to observe” means helping them obey, not merely collect knowledge. The mission includes Jesus' teaching about love, holiness, mercy, forgiveness, justice, prayer, truthfulness, and witness. Churches fall short when they seek decisions without long-term formation or teach information without lived obedience. Discipleship requires patient relationships, example, correction, encouragement, and community.

Jesus closes with the promise, “I am with you alway.” The mission is too large for human strength, but the risen Lord accompanies His people to the end of the age. His presence does not remove rejection or sacrifice; it gives courage, wisdom, and hope to continue. Mission begins with Christ's authority, follows His teaching, and depends on His presence.

## Key Lesson

**The risen Jesus sends His followers to make obedient disciples among every people. The mission is grounded in His authority, expressed through baptism and teaching, and sustained by His continual presence.**

## Application

- Who is one person I can intentionally encourage, teach, or walk alongside as a growing disciple of Jesus?

- Examine whether I am merely learning Jesus' commands or actually practicing what He taught.

- Pray for a people group, missionary, or local outreach and choose one practical way to participate in Christ's mission.

## Cross References

- Genesis 12:3

- Acts 1:8

- 2 Timothy 2:2

## Word Study

- **Make disciples (Greek: mathēteuō) —** To bring people into a learning, trusting, obedient relationship with Jesus and help them grow as His followers.

- **Baptizing (Greek: baptizō) —** To immerse or wash; Christian baptism publicly identifies a believer with the triune God and Christ's community.

- **Observe (Greek: tēreō) —** To keep, guard, and obey carefully rather than merely hear or remember.

## Reflection

Jesus calls me not only to learn but also to help others follow and obey Him. I can begin without perfect confidence because His authority is sufficient and His presence accompanies every faithful step.

## Prayer

Risen Lord Jesus, make me a faithful disciple who helps others follow You. Give me love for every people, courage to cross boundaries, patience to teach by word and example, and obedience that makes Your truth visible. Keep me aware of Your presence throughout Your mission. Amen.

translations.KJV: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
translations.WEB: For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
translations.BSB: For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Paul the apostle.

**Original Audience:** Timothy, Paul's younger ministry coworker, with the letter also serving the wider church that would hear and preserve its instruction.

**Purpose of the Book:** To encourage Timothy to remain faithful to the gospel, endure suffering, guard sound teaching, and continue his ministry with courage as Paul's death approached.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Second Timothy presents Paul as a prisoner expecting the end of his earthly ministry. Timothy faced opposition, false teaching, and the shame that Roman society attached to imprisonment and execution. Paul therefore urged him not to be ashamed of Christ or of Paul, but to share in suffering for the gospel by God's power.

The verse follows Paul's reminder that Timothy possessed sincere faith and should “stir up” God's gift. Timothy may have felt the weight of responsibility, personal timidity, and the danger connected with public Christian ministry. Paul's answer was not ridicule. He reminded Timothy that the inner disposition produced by God equips a believer to act faithfully under pressure.

## Study Note

The “spirit of fear” refers to cowardice or shrinking back, not to every feeling of fear. Fear is a normal human response to danger, and Scripture never requires believers to pretend threats are unreal. The problem arises when fear becomes the ruling power that silences truth, abandons responsibility, or leads a person to disobey God. Paul directs Timothy to identify cowardice as inconsistent with what God supplies.

God gives “power”—the strength needed to endure and serve, not permission to dominate others. This power is immediately joined to “love,” which controls how strength is used. Christian courage is not harsh, reckless, or self-important. It seeks the good of God and neighbor, remains patient with difficult people, and is willing to suffer rather than betray the gospel.

A “sound mind” includes self-control, wise judgment, and disciplined thinking. Under pressure, fear can exaggerate danger and narrow attention. God enables believers to think soberly, govern their reactions, and choose faithful action. The three gifts belong together: power without love becomes destructive, love without courage may avoid necessary truth, and both require sound judgment to be expressed well.

## Key Lesson

**God does not call His people to be ruled by cowardice. He supplies courageous strength, self-giving love, and disciplined judgment for faithful action under pressure.**

## Application

- Where is fear currently persuading me to remain silent, avoid responsibility, or disobey a clear instruction?

- Plan one courageous step, then ask how love and wise judgment should govern the way I take it.

- Replace repeated fearful predictions with prayerful, truthful assessment of the situation and God's resources.

## Cross References

- Joshua 1:9

- Romans 8:15

- Ephesians 3:16

- 2 Timothy 1:6–12

- 1 John 4:18

## Word Study

- **Fear / cowardice (Greek: deilia) —** Timidity or shrinking back from duty because of fear; the term carries the idea of cowardice.

- **Power (Greek: dynamis) —** Ability, strength, or effective capacity supplied by God for faithful service and endurance.

- **Love (Greek: agapē) —** Self-giving commitment that seeks another's true good and governs the use of power.

- **Sound mind (Greek: sōphronismos) —** Self-control, disciplined judgment, and the ability to think and act sensibly.

## Reflection

Courage does not mean that I never feel afraid. It means fear does not receive the final authority over my choices. God can supply strength for the task, love for the people involved, and disciplined thinking for the next faithful step.

## Prayer

God of power and love, keep fear from ruling my decisions. Strengthen me to do what is right, fill my courage with compassion, and give me a calm and disciplined mind. Help me speak, serve, and endure faithfully without becoming harsh, reckless, or ashamed of Christ. Amen.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** The psalm is attributed to the sons of Korah, a Levitical family associated with temple music and worship.

**Original Audience:** Israel's worshipping community, especially God's people needing confidence during national danger and upheaval.

**Purpose of the Book:** The Psalms give God's people inspired language for worship, lament, thanksgiving, wisdom, confession, and confidence in His covenant rule.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Psalm 46 pictures a world in upheaval: earth and mountains move, waters roar, nations rage, and kingdoms fall. The exact historical crisis is not identified. That lack of detail makes the psalm usable across many dangers, including invasion, political instability, natural disaster, and personal crisis.

Ancient cities depended on walls, fortified towers, armies, and secure high places for protection. Israel was repeatedly tempted to trust military strength or foreign alliances. The psalm redirects confidence to God Himself. Jerusalem's security did not finally rest in geography or human defenses but in the presence and rule of the LORD of hosts.

## Study Note

A “refuge” is a place to which vulnerable people flee for protection. The verse does not say God merely provides a refuge; God Himself is the refuge. Safety is therefore relational before it is circumstantial. His people run to Him through prayer, trust, obedience, and remembrance of His character when everything around them appears unstable.

God is also “our strength.” He does not only shelter people until danger passes; He supplies the inner and practical ability needed to endure, decide, serve, and remain faithful within trouble. Human resources can fail, and personal strength can be exhausted. The psalmist locates dependable strength outside the self, in the God shared by the worshipping community—“our” refuge and strength.

“A very present help” means help that is readily found, abundantly available, or proven in trouble. The verse does not promise that believers will never face loss or fear; the rest of the psalm assumes severe upheaval. It promises that trouble never makes God absent or inaccessible. His presence may be experienced through prayer, Scripture, wise people, practical provision, courage, or sustaining peace while the crisis continues.

## Key Lesson

**God is not distant when life becomes unstable. He is the secure refuge, sustaining strength, and readily available help of His people within every trouble.**

## Application

- When trouble comes, where do I instinctively run first for security and control?

- Name the present crisis honestly to God and ask for the specific strength needed for today's responsibility.

- Become part of God's practical help by offering presence and support to someone facing difficulty.

## Cross References

- Deuteronomy 33:27

- Psalm 18:1–3

- Psalm 46:7–11

- Nahum 1:7

- Hebrews 4:16

## Word Study

- **Refuge (Hebrew: maḥăseh) —** A shelter or place of trust to which someone flees for safety.

- **Strength (Hebrew: ʿōz) —** Might, power, or the capacity to stand and act.

- **Help (Hebrew: ʿezrâ) —** Assistance or support supplied to someone in need.

- **Trouble (Hebrew: ṣārâ) —** Distress, pressure, or a constricted situation in which a person feels hemmed in.

## Reflection

Trouble can make me feel exposed and alone, but it does not place me beyond God's reach. I can run to Him before panic, remember that strength does not have to originate in me, and receive the help needed to remain faithful today.

## Prayer

God, You are my refuge and strength. When circumstances shake what I depend on, draw me quickly to You. Supply wisdom, courage, endurance, and practical help for this trouble, and use me to become a steady source of comfort to others. Amen.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Paul the apostle, with Timothy named alongside him in the letter's opening.

**Original Audience:** The church in Philippi, a Roman colony whose believers had supported Paul's ministry and were experiencing opposition and internal strain.

**Purpose of the Book:** To thank the Philippians, encourage unity and humble joy, strengthen them in suffering, and teach them to live as faithful citizens of heaven.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Paul wrote while imprisoned and uncertain whether he would be released or executed. The Philippians also faced opposition, and chapter 4 addresses tension between two respected women, Euodias and Syntyche. The command about anxiety was therefore not offered from a comfortable life or to people with imaginary problems.

Philippi was a proud Roman colony shaped by military history and loyalty to the empire. The language of a peace that “shall keep” hearts and minds uses a word associated with guarding, an image familiar in a city where soldiers and sentries were visible. Paul redirects confidence from military security to the protecting peace God gives in Christ.

## Study Note

“Be careful for nothing” means “do not be anxious about anything”; it does not mean be careless or unconcerned. Scripture permits wise planning, grief, alertness, and responsible action. Anxiety becomes spiritually harmful when it repeatedly divides attention and makes feared possibilities the controlling reality. Paul does not shame anxious believers. He gives them a practiced alternative.

“In every thing” makes prayer the response to concerns both large and small. “Prayer” describes approach to God in worship and dependence, while “supplication” is a specific request arising from need. “Let your requests be made known” does not suggest God lacks information. It invites believers to name their needs honestly instead of carrying them as private, undefined pressure.

Thanksgiving changes the posture of asking. It recalls God's past faithfulness, recognizes present grace, and prevents prayer from becoming nothing more than a list of emergencies. Thanksgiving does not deny pain or force a person to call suffering good. It places the real problem inside a larger truth: God has been faithful, remains present, and is worthy of trust before the outcome is known.

God promises peace, not immediate control over every circumstance. This peace “passeth all understanding” because it can remain present when circumstances provide no ordinary reason for calm. It “keeps,” or guards, the believer's inner life through Christ Jesus. The practice may need repetition: each time anxiety returns, the concern can again be named, requested, thanked over, and entrusted to God while responsible action continues.

## Key Lesson

**Anxiety is answered by honest, specific, thankful prayer. God may not immediately change the situation, but He gives peace in Christ to guard the believer's heart and mind.**

## Application

- Turn one vague anxiety into a specific written request and bring it plainly to God.

- Add three concrete reasons for thanksgiving before returning to the problem in prayer.

- Take the responsible action available today, then deliberately entrust the uncontrollable outcome to God.

## Cross References

- Psalm 55:22

- Matthew 6:31–34

- John 14:27

- 1 Peter 5:7

- Philippians 4:8–9

## Word Study

- **Careful / anxious (Greek: merimnaō) —** To be troubled by divided concern or pulled in different directions by worry.

- **Supplication (Greek: deēsis) —** An earnest and specific request made because of a recognized need.

- **Thanksgiving (Greek: eucharistia) —** Grateful acknowledgment of God's gifts, character, and past faithfulness.

- **Keep / guard (Greek: phroureō) —** To protect like a military sentry, preventing hostile access to what is under guard.

## Reflection

I do not have to choose between pretending nothing is wrong and being consumed by worry. I can name the need, remember God's faithfulness, ask specifically, and act responsibly. His peace can protect my inner life even before I understand how the situation will end.

## Prayer

God of peace, I bring You every concern that divides my mind. Help me name my needs honestly, remember Your faithfulness with gratitude, and release outcomes I cannot control. Guard my heart and thoughts through Christ Jesus, and guide me in the responsible steps I should take. Amen.

translations.KJV: My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.
translations.WEB: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** James, traditionally identified as the brother of Jesus and a leading elder in the Jerusalem church.

**Original Audience:** Jewish Christians described as the twelve tribes scattered abroad, living away from their homeland and facing social and economic pressure.

**Purpose of the Book:** To teach practical, wholehearted faith that endures trials, controls speech, rejects partiality, cares for the vulnerable, and produces obedient action.

## Historical & Cultural Context

James writes to scattered believers whose faith was being tested by poverty, unequal treatment, conflict, temptation, and uncertainty. His letter resembles Jewish wisdom teaching: it is direct, practical, and concerned with the visible conduct that genuine faith produces in ordinary life.

The KJV word “temptations” can refer here to trials or testing circumstances, not only enticement to sin. Later in the chapter James distinguishes external testing from sinful desire. Trials arrive in “divers,” or many different, forms. Believers do not choose all of them, and the phrase “when ye fall into” suggests that some appear suddenly and surround a person unexpectedly.

## Study Note

“Count it all joy” is a call to deliberate evaluation, not forced happiness. James does not say the trial itself is pleasant, that suffering should be minimized, or that grief is wrong. To “count” means to regard the situation from the perspective of what God can produce through it. Joy can coexist with tears because it rests in God's purpose rather than in the painful event.

The “trying” of faith reveals and strengthens what trust is made of, much as testing exposes the quality of a material. A trial may uncover fears, false dependencies, impatience, or shallow beliefs that comfort had concealed. This exposure is not meant merely to embarrass the believer. Under God's wise care, it becomes an opportunity for faith to move from theory into practiced reliance.

Tested faith “worketh patience.” The word means steadfast endurance—the ability to remain under pressure without abandoning trust or obedience. Patience is not passive resignation. It continues praying, doing good, seeking wisdom, and resisting sinful shortcuts when relief is delayed. The following verse shows that endurance has a maturing purpose, shaping a more complete and stable Christian character.

## Key Lesson

**Believers can face trials with deep joy because God uses tested faith to produce steadfast endurance. The pain is real, but it need not be wasted.**

## Application

- What is the present trial revealing about where I place my security and trust?

- Choose one faithful action to continue even though the pressure has not yet changed.

- Ask God for wisdom and support instead of interpreting the trial as proof that He has abandoned me.

## Cross References

- Romans 5:3–5

- Romans 8:28

- 1 Peter 1:6–7

- Hebrews 10:35–36

- James 1:4–5

## Word Study

- **Count (Greek: hēgeomai) —** To consider, evaluate, or regard something after thoughtful judgment.

- **Divers (Greek: poikilos) —** Various, many-colored, or appearing in different forms.

- **Trying / testing (Greek: dokimion) —** The proving process that demonstrates and strengthens genuineness.

- **Patience (Greek: hypomonē) —** Steadfast endurance—the capacity to remain faithful under pressure.

## Reflection

I do not have to pretend that a trial feels good in order to trust that God can use it. I can grieve honestly while asking what faithfulness looks like today. Endurance grows as I continue obeying instead of escaping through despair or sinful shortcuts.

## Prayer

Wise God, meet me in the trials I did not choose. Give me honest joy rooted in Your purpose, reveal what needs to change in me, and strengthen my faith under pressure. Produce patient endurance, guide my next act of obedience, and keep me from wasting pain through bitterness or unbelief. Amen.

translations.KJV: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
translations.WEB: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
translations.BSB: But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Paul the apostle, writing with the assistance of Tertius, who served as the letter's scribe.

**Original Audience:** Believers in Rome from both Jewish and Gentile backgrounds who needed unity in the gospel and practical instruction for life together.

**Purpose of the Book:** To explain the gospel of God's righteousness in Christ, unite Jewish and Gentile believers, and show how God's mercy produces a transformed life.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Romans 5 explains the results of being justified by faith: peace with God, access to grace, hope of glory, and confidence even in suffering. Paul then emphasizes the helpless condition from which people are saved. Humanity is described as weak, ungodly, sinful, and opposed to God.

In the honor-conscious Roman world, benefactors often gave to people considered worthy, useful, or likely to return favor. Paul contrasts ordinary human calculation with God's astonishing generosity. Christ did not wait for humanity to become respectable or friendly toward God before He acted.

## Study Note

“But God” turns attention away from human inability to divine initiative. The gospel begins with what God has done, not with people improving themselves enough to deserve help. “Commendeth” means demonstrates or proves. God's love is not left as an abstract claim; He makes it visible in a specific historical act—the death of Christ.

“While we were yet sinners” describes the timing and the objects of that love. Christ did not die for people who had already repaired their relationship with God. He died for those actively marked by sin and unable to remove their guilt. This does not make sin unimportant; it shows the depth of grace that confronts sin at its worst and provides the costly remedy.

“Christ died for us” means His death was on behalf of sinners and for their saving benefit. In the wider argument of Romans, Jesus bears judgment, reconciles enemies to God, and opens the way to a new life. The cross therefore defines divine love more accurately than changing circumstances or feelings do. When believers question whether God loves them, they are directed to a completed act outside themselves.

## Key Lesson

**God proves His love through Christ's death for undeserving sinners. Salvation begins with divine grace, not with human worthiness or self-improvement.**

## Application

- When I doubt God's love, return to the objective evidence of the cross rather than judging by present circumstances.

- Confess sin honestly, trusting that grace does not require me to hide or make myself worthy first.

- Show costly love to someone who cannot repay me or improve my reputation.

## Cross References

- Isaiah 53:4–6

- John 3:16

- Romans 3:23–26

- Ephesians 2:4–5

- 1 John 4:9–10

## Word Study

- **Commendeth / demonstrates (Greek: synistēmi) —** To show, establish, or provide convincing proof of something.

- **Sinners (Greek: hamartōlos) —** People whose lives are marked by sin and who stand in need of reconciliation with God.

- **For us (Greek: hyper hēmōn) —** On our behalf or for our benefit, emphasizing the representative and saving purpose of Christ's death.

## Reflection

God's love is not a reward for the best version of me. The cross shows that He acted when I was undeserving and unable to rescue myself. I can stop hiding, receive grace with humility, and allow that costly love to reshape how I treat others.

## Prayer

Gracious God, thank You for proving Your love through the death of Christ while I was still a sinner. Keep me from trying to earn what You freely give or hiding what Your grace can forgive. Root my assurance in the cross and teach me to love others sacrificially. Amen.

**KJV Study Guide**

*“Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Moses is the central speaker and traditional author of Deuteronomy; the final account of his death was preserved by another inspired writer.

**Original Audience:** The Israelites preparing to enter the Promised Land after the wilderness generation had died.

**Purpose of the Book:** To renew Israel's covenant commitment, restate God's law, and prepare a new generation to live faithfully in the land He promised.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Moses spoke these words near the end of his life on the plains of Moab. Israel stood east of the Jordan, preparing to enter Canaan without the leader who had guided them out of Egypt. Moses publicly announced that Joshua would lead them and that the nations occupying the land would be confronted.

Israel's fear had historical weight. Forty years earlier, the previous generation focused on fortified cities and powerful inhabitants and refused to trust God's promise. Now the new generation faced a similar decision. Courage would not come from denying the enemy's strength but from remembering that the LORD who defeated Egypt and sustained them in the wilderness would go with them.

## Study Note

“Be strong and of a good courage” calls for steady, obedient resolve. The command does not ask Israel to create confidence from personality or military advantage. Their strength was rooted in God's covenant promise and proven faithfulness. Biblical courage is not self-confidence detached from God; it is the willingness to obey because God is trustworthy.

“Fear not, nor be afraid of them” names the real focus of Israel's anxiety—the people and obstacles ahead. Fear becomes distorted when the visible threat fills the whole field of attention and God's presence is treated as irrelevant. Moses redirects Israel's sight. The enemies would be encountered, but they would not be encountered alone.

The LORD “doth go with thee.” He does not merely send instructions from a distance; His presence accompanies His people into the assignment. “He will not fail thee” means He will not loosen His hold or abandon His commitment. “Nor forsake thee” assures Israel that leadership transition and unfamiliar territory do not cancel God's covenant faithfulness. The promise supports obedience to God's calling, not every plan people invent for themselves.

## Key Lesson

**Courage grows from God's faithful presence, not from the absence of strong opposition. His people can obey because He does not release or abandon them.**

## Application

- Which visible obstacle has become larger in my thinking than God's presence and faithfulness?

- Recall one past example of God's provision before taking the next difficult step of obedience.

- Support someone entering a new responsibility by reminding them of God's presence and offering practical help.

## Cross References

- Deuteronomy 1:29–31

- Joshua 1:5–9

- Psalm 27:1

- Isaiah 41:10

- Hebrews 13:5–6

## Word Study

- **Be strong (Hebrew: ḥāzaq) —** To be firm, resolute, or strengthened for action.

- **Courage (Hebrew: ʾāmēṣ) —** To be bold, alert, and steadfast in the face of difficulty.

- **Fail (Hebrew: rāphâ) —** To loosen, let drop, or withdraw support.

- **Forsake (Hebrew: ʿāzab) —** To leave, abandon, or desert someone.

## Reflection

A difficult transition can make me focus on what I am losing and what I may face. God's promise redirects me to what does not change: His presence and faithful hold. I can acknowledge the challenge and still move forward in obedience without being ruled by fear.

## Prayer

Faithful LORD, make me strong and courageous in the responsibilities before me. When visible obstacles dominate my thoughts, remind me that You go with me and will not abandon Your people. Keep my confidence rooted in Your promise and guide every step in obedience to Your will. Amen.

translations.WEB: The LORD is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?
translations.BSB: The LORD is my light and my salvation—whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life—whom shall I dread?

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?”*

## Book Background

**Author:** David.

**Original Audience:** The people of Israel and successive worshipping communities who used the psalm for prayer, praise, and confidence in God.

**Purpose of the Book:** The Psalms give God's people inspired language for worship, lament, thanksgiving, wisdom, confession, and trust in His covenant care.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Psalm 27 combines strong confidence with honest longing. David speaks of enemies, armies, false witnesses, and the possibility of abandonment, although the exact historical crisis is not named. The psalm therefore does not arise from a trouble-free life. It shows faith being practiced while danger and uncertainty remain present.

Light was a powerful biblical image for life, guidance, truth, and God's saving presence. Ancient nights could be genuinely dangerous without modern lighting, while fortified shelters offered protection during conflict. David gathers these familiar images and declares that the LORD Himself is his light, salvation, and stronghold.

## Study Note

“The LORD is my light” means God gives direction and drives back the darkness that produces confusion and fear. David does not claim to understand every circumstance. He knows the One who enables him to see what is true and take the next faithful step. God's light also exposes falsehood, including the exaggerated conclusions fear may draw from a real threat.

“My salvation” identifies the LORD as David's rescuer. Salvation here includes deliverance from immediate enemies, while the whole biblical story gives the word its deeper meaning of rescue from sin and death. David's confidence is personal—“my”—but not possessive or self-centered. It reflects covenant trust in the God who has bound Himself faithfully to His people.

The LORD is also “the strength,” or stronghold, of David's life. A stronghold was a secure place that enemies could not easily penetrate. The two questions—“whom shall I fear?” and “of whom shall I be afraid?”—do not deny that frightening people exist. They place every threat beneath a greater reality. Fear may still be felt, but it no longer has unquestioned authority because God defines the believer's safety and future.

## Key Lesson

**Fear loses its ruling position when God is known as light, salvation, and stronghold. Real dangers remain, but none possesses greater authority than the faithful LORD.**

## Application

- Which person, outcome, or uncertainty currently occupies more of my attention than God's character?

- Answer one fearful prediction with a specific truth about God's guidance, rescue, or protection.

- Take the next wise step without waiting for every feeling of fear to disappear.

## Cross References

- Psalm 18:2

- Psalm 56:3–4

- Isaiah 12:2

- John 8:12

- Romans 8:31

## Word Study

- **Light (Hebrew: ʾôr) —** Illumination, life, and guidance that dispel darkness and reveal what is true.

- **Salvation (Hebrew: yēshaʿ) —** Rescue, deliverance, or safety supplied by God.

- **Strength / stronghold (Hebrew: māʿôz) —** A fortified place of safety, refuge, or secure defense.

- **Fear (Hebrew: yārēʾ) —** To be afraid or stand in awe; the context concerns terror before a threat.

## Reflection

Fear often speaks as though a threat is the greatest reality in my life. David reminds me to begin elsewhere: the LORD is my light, rescuer, and secure refuge. I can acknowledge danger honestly while refusing to let it define what is true or decide my next step.

## Prayer

LORD, be my light when fear confuses my thinking, my salvation when I feel threatened, and my stronghold when I feel exposed. Turn my attention from imagined defeat to Your faithful presence, and give me wisdom and courage for the next obedient step. Amen.

translations.WEB: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.”

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** John, a Christian prophet exiled on the island of Patmos, traditionally identified with the apostle John.

**Original Audience:** Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, and through them the wider church enduring pressure to remain faithful to Jesus.

**Purpose of the Book:** To reveal Jesus Christ as the victorious Lord, strengthen churches facing compromise and persecution, and assure believers that God will judge evil and renew creation.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Revelation was written to churches living under the power and propaganda of the Roman Empire. Some believers faced economic pressure, social exclusion, false teaching, and persecution. The book uses visions, symbols, and Old Testament imagery to uncover the spiritual reality behind earthly events and call the churches to patient faithfulness.

Chapter 21 follows the final defeat of evil and the last judgment. John sees a new heaven and new earth and the holy city coming down from God. The goal is not humanity escaping creation forever but God dwelling with His redeemed people in a renewed creation. Verse 4 describes what God's presence will permanently remove.

## Study Note

“God shall wipe away all tears” presents a tender and personal picture. God does not treat human suffering as unimportant or tell the wounded simply to forget it. The image suggests personal comfort and complete healing. The tears produced by grief, injustice, persecution, disappointment, and loss are fully known by Him and will not continue forever.

“There shall be no more death” announces the defeat of humanity's great enemy. Death entered the world through sin and casts its shadow over every generation. In the new creation, Christ's resurrection victory reaches its full public result: death is not merely postponed or made less painful; it is removed. The relationships and life God restores will no longer be threatened by separation.

Sorrow, crying, and pain describe the emotional and physical suffering woven through the present age. Their absence does not mean present grief is imaginary or that Christians should avoid mourning. Jesus Himself wept. Christian hope gives people permission to grieve truthfully while refusing to believe that grief is permanent or ultimate.

“The former things are passed away” means the old order corrupted by sin, death, and suffering will no longer govern reality. This promise is not a guarantee that believers will avoid pain now; Revelation was written to suffering churches. It is assurance that faithfulness is not wasted and evil will not have the last word. Future hope also shapes present life, calling believers to comfort mourners, resist injustice, endure faithfully, and live as citizens of God's coming world.

## Key Lesson

**God will complete His victory by dwelling with His people and removing death, grief, and pain forever. Present suffering is real, but it is not permanent or final.**

## Application

- Bring present grief to God honestly, trusting that He sees every tear rather than requiring me to hide it.

- Comfort someone who is suffering through patient presence instead of offering quick or shallow explanations.

- Let the certainty of God's renewed creation strengthen faithfulness when obedience is costly or results seem delayed.

## Cross References

- Isaiah 25:8

- Isaiah 65:17–19

- John 11:25–26

- 1 Corinthians 15:54–57

- Revelation 21:1–5

## Word Study

- **Wipe away (Greek: exaleiphō) —** To remove, erase, or wipe completely, emphasizing the thoroughness of God's comfort.

- **Sorrow (Greek: penthos) —** Deep mourning or grief, especially the sorrow associated with death and loss.

- **Pain (Greek: ponos) —** Pain, distress, or exhausting hardship.

- **Passed away (Greek: aperchomai) —** To depart or go away; the former order loses its place permanently.

## Reflection

The pain I see and experience is not the world as God will finally leave it. He knows every tear and promises a future in which death and suffering have no place. I can grieve honestly today while allowing that promised ending to strengthen hope, compassion, and endurance.

## Prayer

God of all comfort, hold me and others who are grieving. Keep me from shallow answers, and make me patient and compassionate in the presence of pain. Fix my hope on the day You will remove death, sorrow, and suffering forever, and help me live faithfully in light of Your coming renewal. Amen.

translations.KJV: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
translations.WEB: The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
translations.BSB: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** David.

**Original Audience:** The people of Israel and successive worshipping communities learning to seek, praise, and trust the LORD in trouble.

**Purpose of the Book:** The Psalms give God's people inspired language for worship, lament, thanksgiving, wisdom, confession, and confidence in His covenant care.

## Historical & Cultural Context

The heading links Psalm 34 with the time David escaped from a dangerous situation by pretending to be insane before a Philistine ruler. David had fled from King Saul and was isolated, vulnerable, and afraid. The psalm turns that experience into public testimony, inviting others to seek the LORD and learn from His deliverance.

Psalm 34 is also an alphabetic acrostic, helping worshippers remember its wisdom and praise. It does not claim that righteous people avoid all suffering. Verse 19 states plainly that they have many afflictions. The emphasis is that God hears, draws near, sustains, and ultimately delivers His people within their distress.

## Study Note

“The LORD is nigh” directly challenges the feeling that suffering proves God is distant. Nearness does not always mean the immediate removal of the painful circumstance. It means the suffering person is seen, heard, and accompanied by the covenant God. His presence is especially precious when other sources of security have failed.

A “broken heart” describes more than temporary disappointment. It pictures the inner person crushed by grief, loss, failure, or deep distress. Scripture does not romanticize brokenness or suggest people should seek pain for its own sake. It assures those who have been brought low that their condition does not repel God. The proud may resist dependence, but the broken often know clearly how much they need Him.

A “contrite spirit” is crushed or humbled. It may include repentance over sin, but in this psalm it also fits the spirit wounded by affliction. God “saveth” such people—He rescues, preserves, and brings them through. Deliverance may be immediate, gradual, expressed through sustaining grace, or completed in resurrection. The promise is not that every wound closes quickly, but that broken people are not abandoned to destruction.

## Key Lesson

**Brokenness does not drive God away. He draws near to the crushed and humble, sustains them in their pain, and acts for their ultimate rescue.**

## Application

- Tell God honestly where my heart feels crushed instead of hiding pain behind strength or activity.

- Offer quiet presence and practical care to a brokenhearted person without rushing their healing.

- If grief feels overwhelming or persistent, seek support from trusted people and appropriate professional care.

## Cross References

- Psalm 51:17

- Psalm 147:3

- Isaiah 57:15

- Matthew 5:4

- 2 Corinthians 1:3–4

## Word Study

- **Nigh / near (Hebrew: qārôb) —** Close at hand or readily present, emphasizing God's accessibility to the suffering.

- **Broken (Hebrew: shābar) —** To break, shatter, or crush; used here for deep inward distress.

- **Contrite / crushed (Hebrew: dakkāʾ) —** Beaten down, crushed, humbled, or deeply wounded in spirit.

- **Saveth (Hebrew: yāshaʿ) —** To rescue, deliver, preserve, or bring into safety.

## Reflection

When my heart is broken, I may feel that I must repair myself before approaching God. This verse says the opposite: He draws near in the place of need. I can bring Him pain without pretending, receive support without shame, and trust that brokenness will not have the final word.

## Prayer

LORD, draw near to every place in me that feels crushed. Help me speak honestly about pain, receive the care You provide, and wait without despair when healing is gradual. Make me gentle with the brokenhearted, and preserve us in the hope of Your complete deliverance. Amen.

verses.studyNote:
**KJV Study Guide**

*“And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest in me.”*

## Book Background

**Author:** Paul the apostle, with Timothy named alongside him in the letter's opening.

**Original Audience:** The church in Corinth and believers throughout Achaia, including people influenced by teachers who judged ministry by outward strength and impressiveness.

**Purpose of the Book:** To defend the integrity of Paul's ministry, repair his relationship with the Corinthians, encourage generosity, and show how God's power is displayed through weakness.

## Historical & Cultural Context

Some teachers in Corinth presented themselves as impressive “super-apostles” and criticized Paul's suffering, speaking, and apparent weakness. Paul answered by describing hardships that revealed the cost of genuine ministry. He reluctantly mentioned extraordinary revelations but refused to make spiritual experiences the foundation of his authority.

To keep him from pride, Paul received a “thorn in the flesh.” He does not identify it clearly, so interpreters have proposed physical illness, persecution, or another persistent limitation. Paul asked the Lord three times to remove it. Verse 9 records the answer: the weakness would remain, but Christ's grace and power would be sufficient within it.

## Study Note

“My grace is sufficient for thee” does not mean pain is unimportant or that Christians should never pray for relief. Paul prayed repeatedly and specifically. The answer taught him that God's sustaining favor could meet the full demand of the situation even when the desired change did not come. Sufficient grace may appear as endurance, help from others, wisdom, daily provision, or strength to continue faithfully.

“My strength is made perfect in weakness” means Christ's power reaches its intended expression when human self-sufficiency is stripped away. Weakness does not increase Christ's power, as though He were previously limited. It makes the source of effective strength clearer. When success cannot reasonably be credited to talent, image, or control, the sufficiency of Christ becomes more visible.

Paul therefore chooses to “glory” in his infirmities. He is not celebrating suffering for its own sake, refusing treatment, or calling abuse acceptable. He is refusing to treat limitation as proof that God cannot use him. The values of Corinth said weakness disqualified a leader; the gospel showed that surrendered weakness could become the setting in which Christ's power was displayed.

The KJV says the power of Christ may “rest in” Paul; the underlying language can suggest a shelter or dwelling over someone. This does not remove human limits but places them beneath Christ's sufficient presence. Believers can seek healing, develop skills, establish boundaries, and receive professional help while refusing shame over what remains weak. Dependence is not failure; it is the normal posture of grace.

## Key Lesson

**Christ's grace is sufficient when weakness remains. Human limitation does not disqualify a believer; it can become the setting in which His sustaining power is most clearly seen.**

## Application

- What limitation am I treating as proof that God cannot use me or remain faithful to me?

- Ask honestly for relief while also asking for the grace needed if the situation does not change immediately.

- Receive appropriate help and establish wise boundaries instead of confusing dependence on Christ with neglecting available support.

## Cross References

- Isaiah 40:29–31

- 2 Corinthians 4:7–10

- Hebrews 4:15–16

## Word Study

- **Sufficient (Greek: arkeō) —** Enough to meet the need, satisfy the requirement, or sustain someone through a situation.

- **Strength / power (Greek: dynamis) —** Effective ability or divine power, here belonging to Christ.

- **Rest (Greek: episkēnoō) —** To dwell or spread a shelter over, suggesting Christ's power residing protectively with Paul.

## Reflection

I naturally want weakness removed before I believe I can be useful. Christ may bring healing or meet me with sufficient grace inside an ongoing limitation. I can stop measuring worth by self-sufficiency and let dependence reveal the true source of strength.

## Prayer

Lord Jesus, I bring You the weakness I would rather hide or remove. Grant relief according to Your wisdom, and supply sufficient grace for what remains. Free me from shame and self-reliance, guide me toward wise support, and let Your power become visible through faithful dependence. Amen.

Bear with each other and forgive any complaint you may have against one another. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity.

translations.KJV: Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
translations.WEB: Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
translations.BSB: Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

translations.KJV: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
translations.WEB: Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth.
translations.BSB: Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth.

translations.KJV: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
translations.WEB: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
translations.BSB: All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.

translations.KJV: For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
translations.WEB: For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
translations.BSB: For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

translations.KJV: And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
translations.WEB: Let us consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.
translations.BSB: And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

translations.KJV: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
translations.WEB: Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
translations.BSB: Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.

translations.KJV: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
translations.WEB: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach; and it will be given to him.
translations.BSB: Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.

translations.KJV: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
translations.WEB: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
translations.BSB: Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves.

translations.KJV: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
translations.WEB: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
translations.BSB: Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

translations.KJV: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
translations.WEB: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
translations.BSB: But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.

translations.KJV: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
translations.WEB: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
translations.BSB: But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect,

translations.KJV: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
translations.WEB: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
translations.BSB: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

translations.KJV: Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
translations.WEB: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
translations.BSB: Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

translations.KJV: We love him, because he first loved us.
translations.WEB: We love him, because he first loved us.
translations.BSB: We love because He first loved us.

translations.KJV: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.
translations.WEB: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.
translations.BSB: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.

translations.KJV: And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful.
translations.WEB: He who sits on the throne said, “Behold, I am making all things new.” He said, “Write, for these words of God are faithful and true.”
translations.BSB: And the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” Then He said, “Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”

translations.KJV: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
translations.WEB: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
translations.BSB: To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:

translations.KJV: It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
translations.WEB: It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
translations.BSB: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
